{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=responsibility+artificial+agency+accountability+decision+consequences&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6238138\", \"title\": [\"Accountability Protocol: Decision, Exception, Responsibility\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in organizational and societal decision processes, failures increasingly arise not from technical malfunction but from unresolved boundaries of authority, exception response, and accountability. As AI-mediated decisions spread across organizations, accountability is often addressed through legal liability, ethics guidelines, or ad hoc managerial responses. This paper argues that such approaches fail to capture a deeper structural problem: accountability collapses when decision authority, exception response, and responsibility are not coherently aligned. We conceptualize accountability as a protocol rather than a role or rule, and examine how responsibility becomes displaced onto individuals or functions when decision boundaries are undefined. The paper demonstrates why existing organizational roles cannot absorb this burden and why accountability must be designed as part of decision infrastructure. This paper does not advocate technological restraint, but seeks to clarify the structural conditions under which accountability protocols become necessary.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6238138\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"title\": [\"Determining Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence-Based Security Decision Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The chapter discusses the determination of who is responsible when artificial intelligence is used for security decision making within complex organizational environments. It looks at how accountability is shared among system designers, vendors, deployers, and human operators when AI-driven tools are used to influence detection actions, prioritization, and response. The chapter investigates legal principles explaining the relationship between control, foreseeability, and duty of care, along with regulatory requirements for human oversight and governance. {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=mechanisms+of+consequence-sensitive+agency+and+ethical+accountability+in+reinforcement+learning+agents&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.35802/227608\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.35802/227608\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6793998\", \"title\": [\"UG-CPPO: Uncertainty-Gated LLM Infusion for Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning Trading Agents\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Recent work on hybrid Reinforcement Learning-Large Language Model (RL-LLM) trading agents, notably FinRL-DeepSeek [Benhenda, 2025], has revealed a counterintuitive empirical finding: increasing LLM signal infusion strength systematically degrades agent performance, even at perturbation magnitudes as small as 0.1%. We hypothesize that a key factor in this degradation is the absence of epistemic uncertainty estimation on LLM outputs: the agent has no mechanism to distinguish a high-confidence financial signal from an unreliable hallucination. Drawing inspiration from Monte Carlo Dropout techniques in medical imaging uncertainty quantification [Gal and Ghahramani, 2016], we propose UG-CPPO (Uncertainty-Gated CVaR-PPO), a novel architecture that dynamically gates LLM signal infusion based on prompt-ensemble-derived uncertainty. We query the LLM with N =5 semantically diverse prompts per news article and compute the standard deviation σ across responses; when σ exceeds a threshold τ , the gate closes and the signal is suppressed. We apply this gating mechanism to both the action modifier S f (PPO action perturbation) and the risk modifier R f (CVaR penalty). We evaluate the framework on the FNSPID dataset [Dong et al., 2024] with 28,502 (ticker, date) signals computed via OpenAI gpt-4o-mini, using 10seed evaluation on Nasdaq trading 2019-2023. The gating mechanism achieves the predicted activation rate (34.2% ± 0%, exactly within target [30-40%]) and we demonstrate that LLM uncertainty σ is structurally higher in bear markets (2022: 0.614) than in bull periods (2019: 0.525). However, at our computeconstrained scale (500,000 training steps, 10 stocks), UG-CPPO does not show statistically significant performance improvement over baselines on aggregate metrics (Wilcoxon p &gt; 0.05): cumulative return 36.0% ± 3…

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=computational+models+of+value+divergence+path+dependence+multi-agent+reinforcement+learning&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"EdgeTwin-DRL: Real-Time Counter-UAS Detection and Response Optimization Using Edge-Assisted Digital Twins and Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning.\", \"abstract\": \"The time available for a counter-drone system to detect an unauthorized aircraft and determine an appropriate response can be limited. Although cloud processing remains useful for storage and offline analysis, communication delays may constrain its use in time-critical decision loops. This paper proposes EdgeTwin-DRL, an edge-assisted digital twin framework that integrates multimodal sensing and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for counter-drone detection and response optimization. The digital twin maintains a synchronized representation of the protected airspace using radar, electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR), radio-frequency (RF), and acoustic observations. This synchronized state is used by cooperative DRL actors to adjust computational-resource allocation, detection sensitivity, and candidate countermeasures, while a model-based forward-evaluation assesses proposed responses before they are passed to the simulated response pathway. The framework is evaluated in a simulation testbed in which the RF sensing models are calibrated and independently validated using publicly available datasets, while the remaining sensing components are parameterized using published experimental measurements. Within this calibrated simulation environment, EdgeTwin-DRL achieved a false-positive rate of 1.4% and reduced mean detection-to-response latency by up to 72% relative to the Cloud-DRL baseline and by 26% relative to the MAPPO baseline without calibrated, environment-dependent sensing under the communication and computational assumptions used in the simulator. The evaluation was conducted across modeled urban, suburban, and open-field conditions. These results demonstrate the comparative performance of the proposed architecture within the simulated environment and motivate further investigation of edge-assisted digital twins for counter-drone decision support.
